A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Maule earthquake rupture was a large, but not exceptional seismic event in the context of a long-term structural evolution of the forearc.

the shallow crustal normal structures in the Chilean Coastal Corillera are a product of a long-term interplay between the interseismic and coseismic deformation of the megathrust, with the latter being the main driver for the structural style of the forearc.

the shallow crustal normal faulting in the Maule region has been active throughout at least the Quaternary, and that this deformation pattern is not exclusive of this region but can be found elsewhere along the Chilean coast.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the shallow forearc deformation pattern of the Maule region, and probably of the entire Chilean forearc, is not a product of a single megathrust seismic cycle, but rather the outcome of multiple, interseismic and coseismic deformation events.
the structural grain in the shallow crust of the Maule region is dominated by a complex pattern of kilometer-scale normal structures, with reverse faults being subordinate and randomly distributed.

the shallow forearc deformation pattern is not necessarily controlled by a single, dominant, and persistent tectonic regime but rather by a complex interplay between the interseismic, coseismic, and interplate deformational styles.
